theme: Public-health and mobility indices: Google/Apple mobility archives, Cuebiq, SafeGraph/Advan/Dewey samples, Placer.ai-like foot traffic, mobility datasets by city

candidates.name: COVID19_mobility (ActiveConclusion)
candidates.what_it_holds: Archived aggregator mirroring four mobility sources as CSV/xlsx/zip: Google COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports (global, US, Brazil, Europe, Asia/Africa, Americas/Oceania breakdowns), Apple Mobility Trends (worldwide + US), Waze Local Driving Trends (country/city), and TomTom Traffic Index, plus a merged Apple+Google summary. Google data through 15 Oct 2022, Apple through 14 Apr 2022, Waze retired Jul 2022. MIT license, archived/no longer updated.
candidates.why_useful: Single mirror of both Google and Apple's own mobility-report CSVs (the raw category/place-type mobility deltas), which are gone from Google/Apple's own sites now; a longer, city/country-level baseline for travel-mobility shocks and a template for what fields exist (retail&recreation, transit, workplaces, residential) that could be re-anchored against 2026 alt-data. Relevant to gap #5 (engagement/mobility proxies) and #11 (event/shock studies).
candidates.geography: Global with country, region, and US-state granularity
candidates.time_coverage: Feb 2020 - Oct 2022 (Google), through Apr 2022 (Apple), through Jul 2022 (Waze)
candidates.size_hint: Multiple CSV/xlsx/zip files per source, hundreds of MB aggregate across the repo history

candidates.name: covid-19-open-data (Google Cloud Platform)
candidates.what_it_holds: Google's own official open-data project; includes mobility.csv / mobility.json (hosted at storage.googleapis.com/covid19-open-data/v3/) with daily movement-category deltas keyed to a harmonized location-key table spanning country, admin1 (state/region), admin2 (county), and locality levels, resolving ISO/NUTS/FIPS mismatches. Archived by owner Nov 2024; data frozen since updates halted 15 Sep 2022. CC BY license on outputs.
candidates.why_useful: The authoritative, best-documented version of the same Google mobility signal as the ActiveConclusion mirror, with a clean harmonized geography key across country/state/county/locality that is far easier to join to other panels (e.g., Eurostat, TSA, FRED) than the raw report PDFs Google used to publish. Useful as a validated historical baseline for movement-vs-travel-demand relationships and as a schema template for any new mobility index construction.
candidates.size_hint: mobility.csv is a large multi-GB time series across all location keys; per-location subsets available
candidates.license: CC BY (outputs); underlying source data under Google's own ToS
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Related to Google Trends already held (not point-in-time) but this is a different signal (movement, not search)

candidates.name: COVID19USFlows (GeoDS Lab, UW-Madison)
candidates.what_it_holds: Daily origin-destination population flow CSVs derived from SafeGraph mobile-location trajectories, at census-tract, county, and state scale for the entire US, Jan 2019 through at least Apr 2021 (pre-pandemic baseline included). Tract-level files split into 20 parts per date for size. Published alongside a Scientific Data (2020) paper; MIT licensed; includes Python download/merge utilities. Split across multiple linked GitHub repos due to size limits.
candidates.why_useful: A genuine SafeGraph-derived mobility flow dataset committed to GitHub (not just a licensed sample) with county- and state-level granularity and a 2019 pre-pandemic baseline year — directly useful for calibrating a travel-mobility-to-nights elasticity model, and for testing whether short-term-rental demand co-moves with general population flow shocks (hurricanes, events). Fills part of gap #5/#11 and is a concrete method template (SafeGraph flow construction) relevant to gap #17 (methods/nowcasting with mixed-frequency mobility data).
candidates.size_hint: Large multi-file CSV set; tract-level split into 20 files per date across the calendar range

candidates.name: COVID19USFlows-WeeklyFlows (GeoDS Lab, UW-Madison)
candidates.what_it_holds: Weekly-aggregated companion to COVID19USFlows: SafeGraph-derived origin-destination visitor/population flow CSVs at census-tract, county, and state scale, Jan 2019 through 2021. MIT licensed.
candidates.why_useful: Weekly cadence is a better match to the pitch's mixed-frequency nowcasting cadence than the daily version and is smaller to work with; same value case as the daily-flows repo above (SafeGraph mobility as a demand-shock and elasticity calibration input, gap #5/#11/#17).
candidates.size_hint: Multiple CSV files, weekly cadence, split by geography and repo size limits
candidates.last_activity: part of the same actively-cited GeoDS Lab research initiative

candidates.name: DL-COVID-19 (Descartes Labs mobility index)
candidates.what_it_holds: Descartes Labs' mobility statistic (m50: median max-distance moved per day by a typical device; m50_index: percent of Feb-Mar 2020 baseline) at US state (admin1) and county (admin2) level with FIPS codes, provided in NDJSON, long-format CSV, and wide-format CSV (dates as columns). Starts 2020-03-24, CC BY 4.0 licensed, 400+ commits with regular releases.
candidates.why_useful: An independent, non-SafeGraph, non-Google mobility index at daily county granularity with a clean, well-documented, actively-maintained-looking commit history — useful as a cross-check series against the SafeGraph/Google flow data above, and as another distance-moved proxy for gap #5/#11 travel-shock studies.
candidates.size_hint: Daily CSV/NDJSON per state+county, hundreds of rows per day, multi-year

candidates.name: COVIDExposureIndices (PlaceIQ Location Exposure/Device Exposure Index)
candidates.what_it_holds: PlaceIQ-sourced smartphone movement exposure indices: Location Exposure Index (LEX, cross-geography device co-visitation share) and Device Exposure Index (DEX, commercial-venue co-visitation, with income/education/race-quartile splits), published twice weekly (Wed/Sat) as compressed CSVs at state (51), county (~2,000), and CBSA level, 2020-01-20 through 2021-08-24 (discontinued). Underlies Couture/Dingel/Green/Handbury/Williams, Journal of Urban Economics 2021; IRB-approved (UC Berkeley / U Chicago).
candidates.why_useful: A third independent commercial-mobility provider (PlaceIQ, a SafeGraph/Advan/Cuebiq peer) with CBSA-level granularity and demographic splits not present in the Google/Apple/SafeGraph series above — useful for city-level (CBSA) foot-traffic/visitation cross-checks and as a template for how commercial location-data vendors structure exposure/visitation indices, relevant to gap #2 (realized occupancy proxies) and #5/#11.
candidates.size_hint: 154 stars, 335 commits; twice-weekly compressed CSVs across the full date range
candidates.license: Academic use with citation requirement (Journal of Urban Economics 2021 paper)

notes: WebSearch tool ran out of its session-wide quota (200/200) before this scout could run any of its own searches — every WebSearch call returned an error with zero results, apparently because other parallel scouts in this sweep consumed the shared budget first. Worked around this by using WebFetch directly against repos recalled from training knowledge (COVID-era mobility mirrors are a well-known, stable category) and verifying each one's README/description live. This means coverage here is narrower than a full search pass would give: true SafeGraph/Advan/Dewey Data *sample* repos (SafeGraph's own GitHub org has no public repos; Advan and Dewey Data are paid-access marketplaces with no obvious open GitHub mirrors found), Cuebiq mobility data (no public GitHub mirror found or recalled — Cuebiq access is licensed/academic-application-only), and Placer.ai-style foot-traffic data (proprietary, no open mirror known) could not be searched for and may exist on GitHub without my knowledge. Also could not confirm: an Unacast county social-distancing scoreboard repo (existed publicly in 2020 but the org's current repo list no longer shows it — likely deleted, so excluded as a dead link), an OpenTable state-of-industry-data repo (wrong path, could not find correct one), and a Foursquare Open Source Places GitHub mirror (the 2024 Foursquare Open Source Places dataset is real but appears to be distributed via S3/HuggingFace/AWS Open Data rather than a discoverable GitHub repo under the foursquare org). RECOMMENDATION for a follow-up scout: if the WebSearch budget resets, re-run this theme with actual search queries — likely to surface (a) more recent (2023-2026) commercial foot-traffic sample repos, (b) Wayback-Machine-scraped Google/Apple mobility report PDFs for periods this scout's known mirrors don't cover, and (c) city-specific foot-traffic-by-neighborhood datasets that would map more directly to the Inside Airbnb 13-city panel than these US-county/state COVID-era series do. All six candidates found are COVID-era (2019-2022) archives; none are live/current mobility feeds, so their direct forecasting value for FY26/FY27 ABNB quarters is limited to elasticity calibration and event-shock methodology rather than as a current input.
